about: The acclamation joins the cry of the seraphim in Isaiah’s vision (Is 6:3) to the words of the crowd welcoming Christ into Jerusalem (Mt 21:9). The threefold Sanctus praises the Lord God of hosts, whose glory fills heaven and earth. The Benedíctus blesses Him who comes in the name of the Lord.

seg.nr: The Preface comes to its end. The priest joins his hands before his breast and bows as he recites the Sanctus. At low Mass he says it audibly while the server rings the bell. At sung Mass the priest recites the same text quietly while the choir sings. The faithful may join the singing. At the words “Benedíctus qui venit in nómine Dómini” the priest straightens up and signs himself with the cross from forehead to breast. After completing his own recitation he begins the Canon, said silently apart from a few sentences spoken aloud. The priest does not wait for the choir to finish. The Gregorian Sanctus and Benedictus are sung continuously. With other musical settings the Benedictus follows the Consecration. Singing ceases during the Consecration.

seg.tr: Holy, Holy, Holy Lord God of hosts.

ex.w006: Hebrew “Sábaoth” entered Latin without inflection and means “of hosts”.

seg.tr: Heaven and earth are full of Your glory.
Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord.

ex.w017: Latin leaves “est” unspoken: “Benedíctus [est] qui venit” — “blessed [is] he who comes”.
ex.w019: Read as the present: the One who is coming. The perfect “vēnit” is spelled the same and differs only in the length of the first vowel.
